figures.caption: lerobot is an open-source library for end-to-end robot learning. It covers the entire stack, from middleware motor interfaces to large-scale data collection and dataset streaming, supporting an optimized inference stack, scalable implementations of SOTA robot learning algorithms, and providing support for training custom models as well as easily reusing pre-trained ones.
figures.headline: lerobot covers motor interfaces, data streaming, optimized inference, robot learning algorithms, and pretrained models in one library.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: (A) Low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms, using consumer-grade parts and 3D-printable designs. (B) Decentralized efforts to collect expert demonstrations in the form of trajectories surpassed centralized efforts for the collection of large amounts of real-world robotics data.
figures.headline: Low-cost open arms cost a fraction of industrial ones, and decentralized demonstration collection surpassed centralized collection.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 shows how fully accessible teleoperated platforms such as the SO-100, SO-101 (jointly referred to as SO-10X, (Knight et al., 2024)) and ALOHA-2 (Aldaco et al., 2024) can cost down to a fraction of closed-source, industrial-grade robots such as the Franka Emika Panda arm.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Numbers and trends of downloads, datasets, and episodes by robot type over time. The number of episodes in each dataset has been explicitly tracked starting in October 2024 only. For completeness, we report the top-5 robots grouped in Other, for each of the metrics considered, in Table 4.
figures.headline: Franka Emika Panda and xArm lead in downloads, while low-cost community arms account for 50%+ of contributed datasets.
citing_sentences: Open datasets are available for downloads, and Figure 5(a) shows the evolution of the number of downloads over time, with a breakdown of the share of downloads per robot type (Table 1(b)) and per robot type over time (Figure 5(b), see Appendix C for further details).

Despite lerobot only supporting a limited number of robots (grouped under the Other tag in Figure 5(a) and Figure 5(e)), datasets collected for other platforms such as the Franka Emika Panda and xArm lead in the number of downloads and size of the datasets collected (Figure 5(e)).

Conversely, platforms such as the SO-10X are increasingly featured in small-scale decentralized community efforts powered by the accessibility of (1) the hardware platforms used and (2) LeRobotDataset format, with 50%+ of the datasets contributed being collected directly on the SO-10X platforms (Figure 5(d)).

figures.caption: The different robot learning algorithms currently supported by lerobot.
figures.headline: The supported algorithms cover reinforcement learning, behavioral cloning, and multi-task policies.
citing_sentences: lerobot supports reference implementation for multiple SOTA robot learning algorithms, providing useful baselines for experimentation and accessible models across RL, such as HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2024) and TD-MPC (Hansen et al., 2022) and BC, both for single-task ACT (Zhao et al., 2023), Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2024) and VQ-BET (Lee et al., 2024), and multi-task models such as $\pi_{0}$ (Black et al., 2024) and SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) (Figure 6).

figures.caption: Numbers and trends of uploads and downloads of robot learning models by policy type over time. TD-MPC (Hansen et al., 2022), HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2024) and VQ-BET (Lee et al., 2024) are absent from all visualizations as they are not typically uploaded by users.
figures.headline: A single policy type dominates uploads, while three methods are absent from all plots because users do not typically upload them.
citing_sentences: lerobot offers support for custom models too, grouped together under the Other tag in Figure 7.

ACT (Zhao et al., 2023) is a particularly popular model dominating the number of uploads (Figure 7(a)), consistenly ranking as one of the most popular policies trained (Figure 7(b)) and used (Figure 7(d)).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Overview of the generalized inference schema supported by lerobot, whereby a remote server can be used to host compute-expensive policies for inference, while the robot client receives a stream of the actions chunks to enact. The schema provides scalability and flexibility through the possibility to fully customize the function $f$ used to aggregate overlapping chunks.
figures.headline: A remote server hosts costly policies and streams action chunks to the robot client, which aggregates overlapping chunks with a customizable function.
citing_sentences: lerobot defines a custom inference stack which is designed to decouple action prediction (inference) from action execution (control), at both the physical and logical level (Figure 8).

abstract: Robotics is undergoing a significant transformation powered by advances in high-level control techniques based on machine learning, giving rise to the field of robot learning. Recent progress in robot learning has been accelerated by the increasing availability of affordable teleoperation systems, large-scale openly available datasets, and scalable learning-based methods. However, development in the field of robot learning is often slowed by fragmented, closed-source tools designed to only address specific sub-components within the robotics stack. In this paper, we present lerobot, an open-source library that integrates across the entire robot learning stack, from low-level middleware communication for motor controls to large-scale dataset collection, storage and streaming. The library is designed with a strong focus on real-world robotics, supporting accessible hardware platforms while remaining extensible to new embodiments. It also supports efficient implementations for various state-of-the-art robot learning algorithms from multiple prominent paradigms, as well as a generalized asynchronous inference stack. Unlike traditional pipelines which heavily rely on hand-crafted techniques, lerobot emphasizes scalable learning approaches that improve directly with more data and compute. Designed for accessibility, scalability, and openness, lerobot lowers the barrier to entry for researchers and practitioners to robotics while providing a platform for reproducible, state-of-the-art robot learning.

sections.body: The introduction contrasts explicit models, which need analytical descriptions of rigid-body kinematics and contact, with implicit models learned from data. It argues that the robot learning ecosystem is fragmented: middleware is often tailored to specific robots, and datasets lack common formats. lerobot is presented as a vertically integrated library with four parts: a Python middleware API for motor control, the LeRobotDataset format for multimodal recording and streaming, an inference stack that decouples action planning from control execution, and PyTorch implementations of robot learning methods.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Robot learning tools are fragmented, so the authors present lerobot, an open-source library spanning the full stack from motor control to datasets.

sections.body: The background contrasts explicit models, built from modular perception, planning, and control pipelines, with implicit models that map observations directly to actions. It reports that reinforcement learning with prior data, learned reward classifiers, and human interventions reached near-perfect success rates within 1-2 hours of real-world training. Behavioral cloning learns from demonstrations, often with generative models such as variational auto-encoders, diffusion models, or flow matching. The section then lists practical challenges: middleware tailored to specific platforms, varied dataset formats, and implementation differences that can cause significant variance in results.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Low-cost open arms cost a fraction of industrial ones, and this accessibility supports decentralized data collection.

sections.body: The features section lists supported platforms, including SO-100 and SO-101 arms, Koch-v1.1, ALOHA-2, and the Reachy-2 humanoid, and describes a shared middleware. As of September 2025, 16K+ datasets from 2.2K+ contributors use the LeRobotDataset format, which supports streaming without a full download. Table 2 reports peak memory of 211.24 MB for ACT and 13.32 GB for pi0 on an RTX 4090. Table 3 reports ACT at about 100-200Hz on high-end GPUs, while pi0 fails to complete inference within the 5s limit on lower-tier devices. The inference stack decouples prediction from control and merges overlapping action chunks with a user-defined function.
sections.heading: Features
sections.headline: lerobot supports several low-cost arms, a shared dataset format with 16K+ datasets, and reference implementations of policies.

sections.body: The simulation section states that lerobot focuses on real-world robotics and trains as much as possible on real-world data, using simulation mainly for systematic evaluation. It adds evaluation support for two benchmarks: LIBERO, with four fixed task suites of 10 tasks each, and Meta-World, with 50 manipulation tasks. Meta-World suites cover multi-task learning (MT10, MT50) and meta-learning (ML1, ML10, ML45). The section describes the benchmarks and the integration, and reports no benchmark scores.
sections.heading: Simulation
sections.headline: Simulation is used only for benchmarking, since the authors find simulation challenging for the contact-rich tasks the library targets.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes lerobot as a unified open-source stack and reports community use: thousands of datasets, hundreds of thousands of episodes, and hundreds of models. The limitations section names three gaps. Robot coverage is incomplete, though support grew from 3 manipulation setups during 2025 to the 8 platforms currently supported. Algorithm coverage is non-exhaustive, and extending it is future work. Inference performance needs low-level optimization such as quantization and graph compilation, which the library does not currently provide. The authors invite community contributions to address these limits.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: lerobot is presented as a unified open stack, with limits in robot coverage, algorithm count, and inference optimization.

sections.body: The appendix gives build guides for the open robots, and Table 4 breaks down the Other category, where 2370 datasets have an unknown robot platform. It describes StreamingLeRobotDataset, which fetches frames on demand through an IterableDataset interface and decodes video with torchcodec. Table 5 compares synchronous and asynchronous inference for the SmolVLA implementation on three real-world SO-100 tasks over 10 test episodes of 60s each. Average success rates are 78.3 for Sync and 73.3 for Async, while total time is 137.5 for Sync and 97.0 for Async. The speedup comes from logical decoupling, since server and client run on the same machine.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists robot build guides, dataset breakdowns, the streaming dataset design, model and inference examples, and a synchronous versus asynchronous comparison.
